claim: Twelve subjects undergoing invasive neurophysiological monitoring for clinical indications viewed still images (15.8° wide) of faces, as well as non-face control stimuli (1 s of continuous display per image).
source: Twelve subjects undergoing invasive neurophysiological monitoring for clinical indications viewed still images (15.8° wide) of faces, as well as non-face control stimuli (1 s of continuous display per image).
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental procedure and subject sample from the manuscript.

claim: Blocks of ten trials (ten consecutive images) were separated by an intermittent gray screen lasting three seconds, serving as a baseline.
source: Blocks of ten trials (ten consecutive images) were separated by an intermittent gray screen lasting three seconds, serving as a baseline.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and baseline condition.

claim: In some of the blocks (12 out of 44), a red dot was presented at the center of the stimulus, and the subjects were pre-instructed to fixate on it.
source: In some of the blocks (12 out of 44), a red dot was presented at the center of the stimulus, and the subjects were pre-instructed to fixate on it.
evidence: This provides specific quantitative details about the experimental conditions.

claim: In the other 32 blocks, no fixation cross was presented, and the subjects viewed the stimuli freely.
source: In the other 32 blocks, no fixation cross was presented, and the subjects viewed the stimuli freely.
evidence: This describes the free-viewing condition in the experiment.

claim: Eye position was monitored by a video eye tracker (EyeLink 1000, SR Research, Ontario, Canada) synchronized with the stimulus-presenting laptop and the iEEG recording station.
source: Eye position was monitored by a video eye tracker (EyeLink 1000, SR Research, Ontario, Canada) synchronized with the stimulus-presenting laptop and the iEEG recording station.
evidence: This describes the methodology for eye tracking.

claim: Saccades verified to be unrelated with eye blinks and within the magnitude range of 1.3° to 3.7° were marked for comparison with the external stimulus displacements.
source: Offline, saccades verified to be unrelated with eye blinks and within the magnitude range of 1.3° to 3.7° were marked for comparison with the external stimulus displacements.
evidence: This describes the selection criteria for saccades included in the analysis.

claim: Both the external displacements and the selected saccades were considerably smaller than the extent of the stimuli (15.8°).
source: Note that both the external displacements and the selected saccades were considerably smaller than the extent of the stimuli (15.8°).
evidence: This is a direct comparison of displacement/saccade magnitudes to stimulus size.

claim: High-frequency broadband activity (HFB, 70–150 Hz) was estimated from the intracranial recordings as a proxy of population mean firing rate.
source: High-frequency broadband activity (HFB, 70–150 Hz) was estimated from the intracranial recordings as a proxy of population mean firing rate (for further details see Golan et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the neural signal measure used and references prior work for justification.

claim: 115 contacts showed significant and considerable visual response to the images (inclusion criteria: p<0.05 Bonferroni corrected and effect size ≥2 baseline standard deviations).
source: 115 contacts showed significant and considerable visual response to the images (inclusion criteria: p<0.05 Bonferroni corrected and effect size ≥2 baseline standard deviations).
evidence: This provides the sample size and selection criteria for visually responsive electrodes.

claim: In early visual areas, both external displacements and saccades produced a subsequent burst of HFB activity, yielding an overall similar activity profile for these two conditions.
source: As can be readily observed, in early visual areas, both external displacements and saccades produced a subsequent burst of HFB activity, yielding an overall similar activity profile for these two conditions.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the data presented in Figure 1.

claim: In higher order areas along the visual hierarchy- areas V4, VO, face-selective and non face-selective high-level visual regions, saccades produced almost no HFB response modulation whereas external displacements of the stimulus were still effective in triggering an HFB activity increase.
source: However, in higher order areas along the visual hierarchy- areas V4, VO, face-selective and non face-selective high-level visual regions, saccades produced almost no HFB response modulation whereas external displacements of the stimulus were still effective in triggering an HFB activity increase.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Multiple sites (36/115) showed significantly greater HFB contribution of external displacements compared to saccades (pFDR < 0.05).
source: Multiple sites (36/115) showed significantly greater HFB contribution of external displacements compared to saccades (pFDR < 0.05), with greater occurrence of significant difference in visual regions anterior to V3: V1,(1/15), V2 (0/11), V3 (3/12), V4 (4/6), VO (2/6), face-selective electrode (6/15) and high-level non face-selective electrodes (10/18), the latter ROI including both ventral and dorsal high-level sites.
evidence: This provides statistical results from the permutation test shown in Figure 2.

claim: The differences showed a significant discrepancy across ROIs (randomization test of independence, χ2(6)=12.64, p=0.004).
source: The differences showed a significant discrepancy across ROIs (randomization test of independence, χ2(6)=12.64, p=0.004).
evidence: This is a statistical test result comparing the distribution of effects across regions.

claim: No site showed a significantly greater HFB increase for saccades compared with external displacements.
source: No site showed a significantly greater HFB increase for saccades compared with external displacements.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the statistical results from Figure 2.

claim: There was a significant linear correlation (r = 0.66, n = 34, p=0.00002) between the peak response latency of external displacements and the equivalent measure for saccades across electrodes.
source: We found a significant linear correlation (r = 0.66, n = 34, p=0.00002) between the peak response latency of external displacements and the equivalent measure for saccades across electrodes.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the latency analysis.

claim: There was no significant difference in the average latencies of these two conditions (a paired t-test across electrodes, t(33) = 1.15, p=0.26, M = 173.3 ± 51.0 ms for external displacements, M = 164.8 ± 53.2 ms for saccades).
source: There was no significant difference in the average latencies of these two conditions (a paired t-test across electrodes, t(33) = 1.15, p=0.26, M = 173.3 ± 51.0 ms for external displacements, M = 164.8 ± 53.2 ms for saccades).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the latency comparison.

claim: The latency results are consistent with a retinal origin of the HFB increases observed following both external displacements and saccades.
source: These results are consistent with a retinal origin of the HFB increases observed following both external displacements and saccades.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the latency data.

claim: The overlap between electrodes showing greater HFB increase to external displacements vs. saccades and those showing greater HFB increase to gaps vs. blinks was far above chance level, with a Sørensen–Dice coefficient of 0.5763 (p=0.000018, random permutation test).
source: The overlap between the two sets of electrodes was far above chance level, with a Sørensen–Dice coefficient of 0.5763 (p=0.000018, random permutation test, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a statistical result comparing the overlap of two sets of electrodes.

claim: All of the ROIs except for V4 were well fit by a linear relation between the blink suppression index and saccade suppression index (r = 0.95, n = 6).
source: All of the ROIs except for V4 were well fit by a linear relation between the two indices (r = 0.95, n = 6).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the correlation analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: V4 was notably above the trend line, showing greater suppression of saccades than expected.
source: V4 was notably above the trend line, showing greater suppression of saccades than expected.
evidence: This is an observation from Figure 4.

claim: In previous human intracranial (iEEG) work (Golan et al., 2016) we found that excitatory broadband high-frequency activity transients, driven by eye blinks, are suppressed in higher-level but not early visual cortex.
source: In previous human intracranial (iEEG) work (Golan et al., 2016) we found that excitatory broadband high-frequency activity transients, driven by eye blinks, are suppressed in higher-level but not early visual cortex.
evidence: This references findings from a prior publication by the same authors.

claim: A key facet of perceived visual stability is the marked difference in the subjective perception of an external stimulus displacement compared to a similar retinal shift caused by a saccade, which likely reflects an active, extra-retinal compensation for the saccade.
source: A key facet of this perceived visual stability is the marked difference in the subjective perception of an external stimulus displacement compared to a similar retinal shift caused by a saccade, which likely reflects an active, extra-retinal compensation for the saccade (Thiele et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a statement about perceptual stability supported by a citation.

claim: The most investigated candidates for the neural underpinning of the perceptual distinction between external stimulus displacements and saccades are dorsal higher-level visual regions, and in particular the middle temporal (MT/V5) and the middle superior temporal (MST) areas, whose neurons were shown to strongly differentiate between external and saccadic movements.
source: The most investigated candidates for the neural underpinning of the perceptual distinction between external stimulus displacements and saccades are dorsal higher-level visual regions, and in particular the middle temporal (MT/V5) and the middle superior temporal (MST) areas, whose neurons were shown to strongly differentiate between external and saccadic movements (Thiele et al., 2002).
evidence: This summarizes prior research findings with a citation.

claim: This response pattern is compatible with the association of MT/MST activity with perceived (versus retinal) motion.
source: This response pattern is compatible with the association of MT/MST activity with perceived (versus retinal) motion (Tootell et al., 1995; Zeki et al., 1993) and was recently linked with input originating from the superior colliculus and arriving in MT through the pulvinar (Ridder and Tomlinson, 1997; Uematsu et al., 2013).
evidence: This connects the response pattern to prior findings with citations.

claim: Early retinotopic visual cortex (V1/V2/V3), in contrast, is usually believed to reflect retinal displacements regardless of whether they were produced by self- or external- motion.
source: Early retinotopic visual cortex (V1/V2/V3), in contrast, is usually believed to reflect retinal displacements regardless of whether they were produced by self- or external- motion (e.g., for a recent demonstration see Meirovithz et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the prevailing view in the literature with a citation.

claim: Multiple conflicting findings have been reported regarding V1 responses to external versus saccadic stimulus displacements.
source: However, this view is not unanimous, and multiple conflicting findings have been reported.
evidence: This acknowledges controversy in the literature.

claim: Several groups have argued for similar responses of V1 to external and saccadic stimulus displacements, implying retinal-like coding of motion in V1.
source: Starting with the pioneering work of Wurtz (1969), several groups have argued for similar responses of V1 to external and saccadic stimulus displacements, implying retinal-like coding of motion in V1 (e.g. Ilg and Thier, 1996; Fischer et al., 1981).
evidence: This summarizes one set of findings from the literature with citations.

claim: Others have reported responses that were mostly compatible with at least some level of extra-retinal modulation in V1.
source: Others have reported responses that were mostly compatible with at least some level of extra-retinal modulation (e.g., Gawne and Martin, 2002; Kagan et al., 2008) and some have argued strongly for differential responses, including very recent work readdressing this old but yet unsettled question (e.g., Troncoso et al., 2015; McFarland et al., 2015).
evidence: This summarizes another set of findings from the literature with citations.

claim: Ventral high-level visual cortex has traditionally been viewed as having extremely large receptive fields.
source: This area, characterized by category-selective responses, has traditionally been viewed as having extremely large receptive fields (see review in Sayres et al., 2010), and therefore insensitive to both small saccades and small external displacements as long as they are not large enough to replace the objects benefiting from foveal acuity (Levy et al., 2001).
evidence: This describes the traditional view with citations.

claim: Findings indicating a release from adaptation following small external stimulus displacements show that much is still unknown regarding whether and how ventral high-level visual cortex handles the rapid stimulus displacements caused by saccades.
source: However, findings indicating a release from adaptation following small external stimulus displacements (Grill-Spector et al., 1999) as well as reports of position-dependent responses (Sayres et al., 2010), show that much is still unknown regarding whether and how ventral high-level visual cortex handles the rapid stimulus displacements caused by saccades.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge based on prior findings with citations.

claim: Recent findings of saccade-related suppression in V4 may suggest that higher-level ventral regions might be affected by saccadic efferent copy as well.
source: Recent findings of saccade-related suppression in V4 (Zanos et al., 2016) may suggest that higher-level ventral regions might be affected by saccadic efferent copy as well.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on a cited finding.

claim: Studies focused on MT without sampling earlier cortical regions cannot preclude the possibility that the observed effects in MT are inherited from the early retinotopic visual areas.
source: In particular, studies focused on MT without sampling earlier cortical regions cannot preclude the possibility that the observed effects in MT are inherited from the early retinotopic visual areas.
evidence: This is a logical inference about limitations of prior studies.

claim: Observing significant differences between saccades and external displacements in studies focused exclusively on V1 does not rule out the possibility that higher-level regions may display a far greater level of differential processing of saccades compared to external displacements.
source: Conversely, observing significant differences between saccades and external displacements in studies focused exclusively on V1 does not rule out the possibility that higher-level regions may display a far greater level of differential processing of saccades compared to external displacements.
evidence: This is a logical inference about limitations of prior studies.

claim: To the best of our knowledge, a direct electrophysiological comparison of saccades and external displacements across the visual hierarchy has not been made yet.
source: However, to the best of our knowledge, such a direct electrophysiological comparison of saccades and external displacements across the visual hierarchy has not been made yet.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature.

claim: Human intracranial EEG recordings (ECoG/SEEG), conducted for clinical diagnostic purposes, often sample the cortex with a substantial anatomical coverage, while still accessing population activity at the millimeter/millisecond spatiotemporal scale.
source: Human intracranial EEG recordings (ECoG/SEEG), conducted for clinical diagnostic purposes, often sample the cortex with a substantial anatomical coverage, while still accessing population activity at the millimeter/millisecond spatiotemporal scale.
evidence: This describes the methodological advantages of the technique used.

claim: In a previous study using intracranial recordings, we found that in high-level visual cortex transient responses to visual interruptions were suppressed when such interruptions were produced by blinks, but not when they were produced by external stimulus blanking.
source: In that study, we found that in high-level visual cortex transient responses to visual interruptions were suppressed when such interruptions were produced by blinks, but not when they were produced by external stimulus blanking (Golan et al., 2016).
evidence: This references findings from a prior publication by the same authors.

claim: In a previous study using intracranial recordings, both kinds of interruptions (blinks and external blanking) elicited similar responses in early visual cortex.
source: In contrast, both kinds of interruptions elicited similar responses in early visual cortex.
evidence: This references findings from a prior publication by the same authors.

claim: With regard to the primary effect we report, which is the appearance of HFB increases in higher-level visual cortex following external displacements but not saccades, we believe a retinal account of the effect is unlikely.
source: Nevertheless, with regard to the primary effect we report, which is the appearance of HFB increases in higher-level visual cortex following external displacements but not saccades, we believe a retinal account of the effect is unlikely.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Low-level retinal discrepancies between saccades and displacements can be expected to have the largest effect on neuronal responses in early stages of the cortical hierarchy and a smaller effect on high order processing.
source: Similar to the case of blink-related responses (Golan et al., 2016), low-level retinal discrepancies between saccades and displacements can be expected to have the largest effect on neuronal responses in early stages of the cortical hierarchy – that are particularly sensitive to such low-level parameters – and a smaller effect on high order processing (see Grill-Spector and Malach, 2004).
evidence: This is a theoretical expectation based on prior work and citations.

claim: The results show the opposite trend to what would be expected from a retinal account, with similar responses to displacements and saccades in V1 and increasing discrepancies between saccades and displacements at higher levels of the hierarchy.
source: However, our results show the opposite trend, with similar responses to displacements and saccades in V1 and increasing discrepancies between saccades and displacements at higher levels of the hierarchy.
evidence: This is a direct interpretation of the observed data pattern.

claim: There are multiple findings of modulation of the early visual cortex activity by saccades in total darkness and even during REM sleep, providing evidence that at least some extra-retinal saccade-related signal arrives at the early visual cortex.
source: There are multiple findings of modulation of the early visual cortex activity by saccades in total darkness (e.g., Sylvester et al., 2005) and even during REM sleep (Uematsu et al., 2013), providing evidence that at least some extra-retinal saccade-related signal arrives at the early visual cortex.
evidence: This summarizes prior findings with citations.

claim: The external displacements employed did not simulate the momentary blurring of the entire visual field caused by saccades.
source: Since the external displacements we employed were simply an update of the stimulus location on an LCD screen, they did not simulate the momentary blurring of the entire visual field caused by saccades.
evidence: This is a description of a limitation of the experimental design.

claim: Momentary reduction in spatial contrast during saccades is a plausible contributor to temporary HFB reductions in early visual areas.
source: Obviously, such a momentary reduction in spatial contrast is a plausible contributor to temporary HFB reductions in early visual areas.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of potential mechanisms.

claim: The finding of diminishing HFB responses to saccades compared to external displacements along the visual hierarchy is compatible with the suppression of saccade-related responses previously observed in non-human primate MT/MST.
source: The finding of diminishing HFB responses to saccades compared to external displacements along the visual hierarchy is compatible with the suppression of saccade-related responses previously observed in non-human primate MT/MST (Thiele et al., 2002).
evidence: This connects the current findings to prior work with a citation.

claim: The concurrent recordings across the visual hierarchy reveal a striking contrast between lower and higher-level cortical regions in representing self-generated versus external stimulus displacements.
source: However, the current findings extend earlier reports in two respects. First, the concurrent recordings across the visual hierarchy reveal a striking contrast between lower and higher-level cortical regions in representing self-generated versus external stimulus displacements.
evidence: This is a direct interpretation of the findings.

claim: The similar HFB increases in early visual cortex following external displacements and saccades indicate that despite the documented extra-retinal effects in V1, this region's activity is strongly perturbed by small saccades, compared with higher-level visual cortex.
source: In particular, the similar HFB increases in early visual cortex following external displacements and saccades indicate that despite the documented extra-retinal effects in V1, this region's activity is strongly perturbed by small saccades, compared with higher-level visual cortex.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The 'unstabilized' nature of early visual cortex provides further evidence that V1 activity is incompatible with the individual's subjective perceptual awareness (as hypothesized by Crick and Koch, 1995).
source: As in the case of blinks (Golan et al., 2016), the 'unstabilized' nature of early visual cortex provides further evidence that V1 activity is incompatible with the individual's subjective perceptual awareness (as hypothesized by Crick and Koch, 1995).
evidence: This connects the findings to a theoretical framework with citations.

claim: The current results extend the observed saccadic suppression effect to ventral high-level visual cortical regions, including face-selective sites.
source: A second advance of the current results is the extension of the observed saccadic suppression effect to ventral high-level visual cortical regions, including face-selective sites.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a novel finding.

claim: The results confirm that in contrast to the traditional view of the category-selective ventral visual cortex as largely position and motion invariant, these areas clearly show a considerable sensitivity to small external displacements.
source: The results further confirm that in contrast to the traditional view of the category-selective ventral visual cortex as largely position and motion invariant, these areas clearly show a considerable sensitivity to small external displacements.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in relation to prior views.

claim: The finding that transient responses to displacement are quenched during saccades indicates that extra-retinal saccade-related information affects not only the dorsal visual processing stream but also the ventral one.
source: Furthermore, the finding that these transient responses to displacement are quenched during saccades indicates that extra-retinal saccade-related information affects not only the dorsal visual processing stream but also the ventral one.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: This result is compatible with the suggestion of an extra-retinal stabilization mechanism in the ventral stream (Leopold and Logothetis, 1998).
source: This result is compatible with the suggestion of an extra-retinal stabilization mechanism in the ventral stream (Leopold and Logothetis, 1998).
evidence: This connects the findings to a prior hypothesis with a citation.

claim: The results support the conclusion of extra-retinal stabilization by directly comparing external displacements and saccades, thus precluding the alternative of a purely passive stabilization achieved through large receptive fields.
source: Our results support this conclusion by directly comparing external displacements and saccades, thus precluding the alternative of a purely passive stabilization achieved through large receptive fields.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the methodological advantage of the study.

claim: When saccades are larger than the displayed object, they are likely to bring new objects into the fovea and thus change the high-level neural responses.
source: When saccades are larger, they are likely to bring new objects into the fovea and thus change the high-level neural responses (DiCarlo and Maunsell, 2000; Hamamé et al., 2014; Podvalny et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about expected effects based on prior work with citations.

claim: The displacement versus saccade contrast does not effectively assess visual regions that are insensitive to both.
source: Another reservation is that the displacement versus saccade contrast does not effectively assess visual regions that are insensitive to both.
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation of the experimental design.

claim: Such regions insensitive to both displacements and saccades may lie at the more anterior end of the ventral high-level visual cortex.
source: Such regions may lie at the more anterior end of the ventral high-level visual cortex (e.g. Figure 3b, rightmost column).
evidence: This is a speculation based on observations in Figure 3b.

claim: The results are limited to HFB activity, and it is possible that single unit activity or slower iEEG frequencies might show different result patterns.
source: Last, it has to be noted that our results are limited to HFB activity: While it is the best iEEG correlate of average spiking rate (Mukamel et al., 2005), it is possible that single unit activity (which was not recorded in our subjects) or slower iEEG frequencies (which we did not analyze due to the limited resolvability of their spatial sources) might show different result patterns.
evidence: This is a statement about limitations of the study with a citation.

claim: The analysis indicates a strong resemblance in how saccade-related and blink-related transients are suppressed along the cortical hierarchy.
source: Finally, our analysis indicates a strong resemblance in how saccade-related and blink-related transients are suppressed along the cortical hierarchy (See Results and Figure 4).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a finding shown in Figure 4.

claim: Along with the psychophysical resemblance between blink and saccadic suppression, these findings suggest that motor-visual pathways informing higher-level visual cortex of blinks and saccades considerably overlap.
source: Along with the psychophysical resemblance between blink and saccadic suppression (Ridder and Tomlinson, 1997), these findings suggest that motor-visual pathways informing higher-level visual cortex of blinks and saccades considerably overlap.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings with a citation.

claim: An interesting possibility is that blinks and saccades are utilizing a single, shared descending pathway.
source: An interesting possibility is that these two oculomotor events are utilizing a single, shared descending pathway.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis.

claim: The hypothesis of a shared pathway is supported by the systematic occurrence of small transient downward-nasalward eye movements during eye blinks.
source: The latter hypothesis is supported by the systematic occurrence of small transient downward-nasalward eye movements during eye blinks (Collewijn et al., 1985).
evidence: This is a supporting argument for the hypothesis with a citation.

claim: From an evolutionary perspective, the pressure to suppress the impact of saccades and eye retractions on vision was exerted already on our eyelidless aquatic ancestors.
source: Furthermore, it is intriguing to note that from an evolutionary perspective (kindly suggested by one of the anonymous reviewers), the pressure to suppress the impact of saccades and eye retractions on vision was exerted already on our eyelidless aquatic ancestors.
evidence: This is a speculative evolutionary argument.

claim: When the need to suppress the visual impact of eye blinks first appeared, a pathway linking extra-ocular activity to suppression of the visual response was probably already present.
source: Hence, when the need to suppress the visual impact of eye blinks first appeared, a pathway linking extra-ocular activity to suppression of the visual response was probably already present.
evidence: This is a speculative evolutionary inference.

claim: The present results leave open the question of the precise mechanism underlying the saccade-related suppression of activity transients in ventral stream representations.
source: However, the present results leave open the question of the precise mechanism underlying the saccade-related suppression of activity transients in ventral stream representations.
evidence: This is a statement about what the study does not resolve.

claim: The mechanism may be a general gating mechanism—suppressing all motion-related transients regardless of saccade direction—or a more specific offsetting by oculomotor motion vectors, similar to that previously described in monkey MT.
source: That mechanism may be a general gating mechanism—suppressing all motion-related transients regardless of saccade direction—or a more specific offsetting by oculomotor motion vectors, similar to that previously described in monkey MT (Thiele et al., 2002).
evidence: This presents alternative hypotheses for the mechanism with a citation.

claim: All patients gave fully informed consent, including consent to publish, according to NIH guidelines, as monitored by the institutional review board at the Feinstein Institute for Medical Research, in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
source: All patients gave fully informed consent, including consent to publish, according to NIH guidelines, as monitored by the institutional review board at the Feinstein Institute for Medical Research, in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical compliance.

claim: Eye position was tracked by an EyeLink 1000 video eye tracker operating at 500 Hz (0.05° RMS resolution).
source: Eye position was tracked by an EyeLink 1000 video eye tracker (EyeLink 1000, SR Research, Ontario, Canada), operating at 500 Hz (0.05° RMS resolution).
evidence: This describes the technical specifications of the eye tracking equipment.

claim: Eye tracking was obtained without head-stabilization, using a head-tracking enabled by a forehead sticker.
source: Eye tracking was obtained without head-stabilization, using a head-tracking enabled by a forehead sticker.
evidence: This describes the eye tracking methodology.

claim: In practice, only little head movement occurred since the patients rested their head on a pillow.
source: However, in practice, only little head movement occurred since the patients rested their head on a pillow.
evidence: This describes the actual conditions during recording.

claim: A standard 9-point calibration was followed by a validation procedure that ensured tracking quality was estimated as 'GOOD' by the eye tracker's acquisition software (no more than 0.5° average error and 1° maximal error across fixation targets).
source: A standard 9-point calibration was followed by a validation procedure that ensured tracking quality was estimated as 'GOOD' by the eye tracker's acquisition software (no more than 0.5° average error and 1° maximal error across fixation targets).
evidence: This describes the calibration and validation procedures for eye tracking.

claim: Periods of no successful tracking or where eye position was estimated to lie outside the stimulus borders were discarded from analysis, as well as the preceding 50 ms and following 250 ms.
source: Periods of no successful tracking or where eye position was estimated to lie outside the stimulus borders were discarded from analysis, as well as the preceding 50 ms and following 250 ms (eye blinks were excluded from this rejection criterion).
evidence: This describes the data exclusion criteria.

claim: Saccades were detected using the built-in saccade detection algorithm of EyeLink 1000, excluding saccade events encompassing blink events.
source: Saccades were detected using the built-in saccade detection algorithm of EyeLink 1000, excluding saccade events encompassing blink events.
evidence: This describes the saccade detection methodology.

claim: Saccade magnitudes were converted from pixels to visual angle based on screen distance (70 cm) and screen pixel density (78.5 DPI).
source: Saccade magnitudes were converted from pixels to visual angle based on screen distance (70 cm) and screen pixel density (78.5 DPI).
evidence: This describes the conversion methodology for saccade magnitudes.

claim: The small (50 pixels) and large (140 pixels) displacements were translated into 1.3 and 3.7 visual degrees.
source: For example, the small (50 pixels) and large (140 pixels) displacements were translated into 1.3 and 3.7 visual degrees.
evidence: This provides specific conversion values for the displacements.

claim: A Finite Impulse Response (FIR) General Linear Model enabled estimating the contribution of each experimental event to the HFB timecourse of each electrode while correcting for overlap artifacts.
source: As in Golan et al. (2016) a Finite Impulse Response (FIR) General Linear Model enabled estimating the contribution of each experimental event to the HFB timecourse of each electrode while correcting for overlap artifacts.
evidence: This describes the statistical modeling approach.

claim: Saccades and displacements were modeled by FIR predictor sets, each set spanning from 300 ms before displacement/saccade offset to 500 ms following displacement/saccade offset.
source: Saccades and displacements were modeled by FIR predictor sets, each set spanning from 300 ms before displacement/saccade offset to 500 ms following displacement/saccade offset.
evidence: This describes the temporal parameters of the FIR model.

claim: Using saccades' onsets instead of offsets produced very similar results.
source: Using saccades' onsets instead of offsets produced very similar results.
evidence: This describes a control analysis.

claim: For the Sørensen–Dice coefficient analysis, only the 108 visually-responsive electrodes obtained from the 11 patients who were included in both this report and in Golan et al. (2016) were used.
source: For this measure, we used only the 108 visually-responsive electrodes obtained from the 11 patients who were included in both this report and in Golan et al. (2016).
evidence: This describes the sample used for a specific analysis.

claim: Statistical testing of the Sørensen–Dice coefficient against chance was done by randomly permuting (100,000 random permutations) the 108 electrode labels within one of the statistical maps.
source: Statistical testing of the resulting index against chance was done by randomly permuting (100,000 random permutations) the 108 electrode labels within one of the statistical maps.
evidence: This describes the statistical testing procedure.

claim: The correlation with V4 removed was tested against chance using a bias-corrected randomization procedure that simulated the null hypothesis by shuffling the datapoints and repeatedly measuring the correlation obtained after removing the data point that most hindered the correlation coefficient in each simulation.
source: Simulating the null hypothesis of no correlation by shuffling the datapoints (Howell, 2015), we repeatedly measured the correlation obtained after removing the data point that most hindered the correlation coefficient in each simulation (i.e., taking the maximal correlation value across all possible single-outlier removals).
evidence: This describes the bias-corrected statistical testing procedure.

claim: The bias-corrected null distribution was centered on 0.29 instead of 0.00.
source: This resulted in a null distribution of the biased correlation coefficient (which was, in our case, centered on 0.29 instead of 0.00).
evidence: This describes the result of the bias-correction procedure.

claim: The data reported here is a product of a reanalysis of the experimental sessions reported in Golan et al. (2016), except for a single subject who was tested later on (patient code P68).
source: The data reported here is a product of a reanalysis of the experimental sessions reported in Golan et al. (2016), except for a single subject who was tested later on (patient code P68, 29 Y/O, female, right hemisphere Lateral Occipital and Fusiform Gyrus seizure onset zones, SOZs excluded from analysis) and three subjects who were excluded from the current report either due to lack of video eye-tracking (P20 and P25) or due to lack of a sufficient number of matching saccades (P46).

claim: In subject P57, the saccade-related activity increase in V1 was preceded by an activity decrease.
source: In subject P57 (Figure 3a), V1 (left column) and MST (right column, an electrode located slightly less than 1 cm anterior to the anatomically defined MST/TO2) sites were recorded simultaneously. In this particular case, the saccade-related activity increase in V1 was preceded by an activity decrease.
evidence: This is an observation from Figure 3a.

claim: The trend of activity decrease preceding saccade-related activity increase in V1 was not sufficiently strong to pass false-discovery rate control when compared with displacements at the group level.
source: This trend was not sufficiently strong to pass our false-discovery rate control when compared with displacements at the group level.
evidence: This is a statement about statistical significance.

claim: In subject P39, recordings from V2 and three face-selective sites may hint at a hierarchical gradient within face-selective sites, with insensitivity to the saccadic displacement at anterior but not posterior FFA and relatively invariant response both to saccades and external displacements in the anterior face patch site.
source: In subject P39 (Figure 3b), a V2 response (leftmost column, responses collapsed over face and non-face trials) is compared with three face-selective sites sampling posterior and anterior FFA (FFA-1 and FFA-2,Weiner and Grill-Spector, 2012) and a probable anterior temporal face patch (rightmost column, see Rajimehr et al., 2009). Beyond replicating the pattern of HFB activity increase in high-level visual regions following external displacements but not after saccades, this particular case may hint at a hierarchical gradient within face-selective sites, with insensitivity to the saccadic displacement at anterior but not posterior FFA and relatively invariant response both to saccades and external displacements in the anterior face patch site.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of observations from Figure 3b with citations.

claim: Since the V4 sample was small (6 electrodes), we cannot unequivocally determine from the current data whether this sample-level deviation reflects that V4, in general, has a particularly strong suppression effect for saccades compared with blinks.
source: However, since our V4 sample was small (6 electrodes), we cannot unequivocally determine from the current data whether this sample-level deviation reflects that V4, in general, has a particularly strong suppression effect for saccades compared with blinks.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of interpreting the V4 result.

claim: Repeating the analysis while using only saccades whose onsets were in the range of 300–700 ms post trial-onset resulted in a highly comparable statistical map with 39/115 electrodes showing significantly greater HFB contribution of external displacements compared to saccades and one V2 electrode showing the opposite effect.
source: Repeating this analysis while using only saccades whose onsets were in the range of 300–700 ms post trial-onset resulted in a highly comparable statistical map (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), with 39/115 electrodes showing significantly greater HFB contribution of external displacements compared to saccades and one V2 electrode showing the opposite effect.
evidence: This describes the results of a control analysis shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: Comparing the saccades with only the small (1.3°) external displacements found qualitatively similar results, yet with a lower number of significant sites (25/115 significant electrodes), likely due to the reduced statistical power of this smaller sample analysis.
source: Last, comparing the saccades with only the small (1.3°, Figure 2—figure supplement 2) or large (3.7°, Figure 2—figure supplement 3) external displacements also found qualitatively similar results, yet with a lower number of significant sites (25/115 and 27/115 significant electrodes, respectively), likely due to the reduced statistical power of these smaller sample analyses.
evidence: This describes the results of a control analysis shown in a supplementary figure.
